issues.legal_issue: A judgment of a single judge in a statutory appeal to a High Court is subject to an intra-court appeal under the court’s charter unless the legislature has removed that right expressly or by necessary implication.
material_facts: The statute provided an appeal from the Tribunal to the High Court, and the High Court’s rules assigned that appeal to a single judge.
The single judge dismissed the statutory appeal, and a further appeal was brought under the High Court’s charter.
issues.conclusion: A statutory appeal heard by a single judge is governed by the High Court’s practice and procedure; if the single judge’s order is a judgment and the legislature has not taken away the further-appeal right, an intra-court appeal lies. The statute at issue did take away that right, as addressed separately.
issues.legal_principle: Under clause 10 of the Letters Patent and section 108 of the Government of India Act, 1915, an appeal to an established High Court is regulated by that court’s practice and procedure. A single judge’s judgment in such an appeal is appealable under the Letters Patent unless the legislature expressly or by necessary implication removes that right. The court relied on National Sewing Thread Co. Ltd. v. James Chadwick & Bros. Ltd., National Telephone Co. Ltd. v. Postmaster-General, R.M.A.R.A. Adaikappa Chettiar v. Ra. Chandrasekhara Thevar, Secretary of State for India v. Chellikani Rama Rao, Maung Ba Thaw v. Ma Pin, and Hem Singh v. Basant Das.

rule.if: statutory_appeal_to_high_court and heard_by_single_judge and single_judge_order_is_judgment and not legislature_removed_further_appeal

predicates.statutory_appeal_to_high_court: A statute provides an appeal to a High Court from an order of a tribunal or court.
predicates.heard_by_single_judge: The High Court assigns and hears the statutory appeal before a single judge.
predicates.single_judge_order_is_judgment: The single judge makes an order that qualifies as a judgment.
predicates.legislature_removed_further_appeal: The legislature expressly or by necessary implication takes away the right to appeal from the single judge’s judgment.

issues.definition: When a statutory appeal is heard by a single judge and the order is a judgment, an intra-court appeal lies if the legislature has not removed that right.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory provision making an order on appeal final excludes a further appeal where the statutory scheme provides an exhaustive process for deciding the relevant disputes.
material_facts: The Act provided an appeal from the Tribunal to the High Court on a substantial question of law.
The Act stated that an order passed on appeal was final and could not be called into question in an original suit, application, or execution proceeding.
The statutory scheme provided a hierarchy of tribunals for resolving disputes under the Act.
issues.conclusion: The finality provision barred a further appeal from the High Court’s order, as well as collateral proceedings challenging it; the Letters Patent appeal was therefore not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 39 and 43 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, read together, make the High Court’s order on appeal final and bar both a further appeal and collateral proceedings. In the context of the Act’s exhaustive statutory scheme, the collateral-proceedings language does not restrict the meaning of “final.” The court relied on Maung Ba Thaw v. Ma Pin, Kydd v. Liverpool Watch Committee, and Secretary of State v. Hindustan Co-operative Insurance Society Ltd.

predicates.statutory_appeal_proceeding: The matter arises from an appeal provided by statute within a statutory decision-making scheme.
predicates.statute_makes_appellate_order_final: The statute describes the order made on appeal as final.
predicates.statutory_scheme_is_exhaustive: The statute establishes an exhaustive process and hierarchy for deciding disputes within its scope.

issues.definition: When an exhaustive statutory process makes an appellate order final, no further appeal lies from that order.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory appeal to a High Court and an intra-court appeal under the High Court’s charter are distinct appeals, and the statutory reference to an appeal does not itself include the charter appeal.
material_facts: The Act provided an appeal from the Tribunal to the High Court, which was decided by a single judge.
A further appeal from the single judge to a Division Bench was sought under the High Court’s charter.
The Act’s finality provision applied to the order passed on the statutory appeal.
issues.conclusion: The statutory appeal and the Letters Patent appeal were different appeals in law and fact; the statutory reference to an appeal did not include the Letters Patent appeal. The court relied on the statutory finality provision to hold that the further appeal was barred.
issues.legal_principle: A Letters Patent appeal is a fresh appeal from the single judge’s order, not a continuation of the appeal initially brought to the High Court. The court relied on sections 39 and 43 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Union of India v. Mohindra Supply Company, and Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd.

predicates.statutory_appeal_to_high_court: A statute provides an appeal to a High Court from an order made by another decision-making body.
predicates.single_judge_decides_statutory_appeal: A single judge decides the statutory appeal in the High Court.
predicates.intra_court_appeal_sought: A party seeks a further appeal within the High Court from the single judge’s decision.

issues.definition: When a single judge decides a statutory appeal and a further intra-court appeal is sought, the two appeals are distinct rather than a single continuing appeal.
